extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers / Men of Letters; literary students and literary intellectuals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for the 'Man of Letters' — what makes a literary hero: qualities of genius, vocation, social responsibility, style, and moral seriousness in writing for wide and lasting influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Living in the inward sphere / Divine Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hero is he who lives in the inward sphere of things, in the True, Divine and Eternal; he discerns and makes manifest the 'Divine Idea of the World.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from Fichte's phrasing: the Man of Letters is sent specially that he may discern for himself, and make manifest to us, this same Divine Idea; whoever 'lives not wholly in this Divine Idea' is not a Literary Man. The writer's work should be aimed at revealing the deeper, permanent reality beneath appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / sincerity / genius (genuineness)
rubrics_metrics.description: What we call 'originality,' 'sincerity,' 'genius' — the heroic quality — signifies that the writer is genuine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuineness means speaking from an inspired, inward place rather than imitation or superficiality. Fichte's contrast ('Bungler, Stumper, Nonentity') warns against partial or spurious engagement with the writer's subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic / Priestly function (revelatory vocation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Man of Letters functions as a Prophet or Priest — a perpetual Priesthood unfolding the Godlike to men and guiding them like a 'sacred Pillar of Fire.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should see themselves as moral/spiritual guides: 'He is the light of the world; the world's Priest.' Their work is not mere entertainment but revelation and guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to Truth and Order (moral seriousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Order is Truth — each thing standing on its basis; smooth Falsehood is Disorder. The writer opposes falsehood and seeks to establish truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly contrasts Truth with Falsehood and Disorder (e.g., discussion of Knox). Literary heroism involves moral seriousness: resisting falsehoods and working to 'extinguish' them in some wise way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasive power and social responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Books persuade and regulate practice; the writer's output has real-world consequences (from household conduct to nation-building).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: popular novels shaping marriages and households ('Celia', 'Clifford'); the Hebrew Book influencing St. Paul's Cathedral. Thus writers must be conscious of and responsible for the social effects of their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic impact as worship (ability to move the heart)
rubrics_metrics.description: True singing/writing is of the nature of worship: the gifted writer's melodious words bring melody into hearts and touch readers as with a 'live coal from the altar.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literature as 'apocalypse of Nature' — revelation of the Godlike. The aim is to move, uplift, and offer something akin to worship through beauty and moral feeling (examples: Shakespeare, Goethe, Milton, Burns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, accuracy and faithful reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer must 'report not falsely' — the eye must report truly, because books function as the 'true University' and shape what others know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because readers depend on books as sources of knowledge and moral guidance, fidelity to truth, accuracy of representation, and clear reporting are essential duties of the literary man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality and timelessness (speaking to all men and times)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Book-writer speaks not to one parish but 'to all men in all times and places'; literature should have comprehensiveness and lasting relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should aim for works that can be read across generations; the 'true reign of miracles' of books lies in linking Past and Present. Strive for ideas and forms that transcend immediate fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endurance through poverty and struggle (ordeal as test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poverty, sorrow, contradiction and worldly distress can be necessary schooling: a man of letters may be 'better for being poor'; the ordeal of chaotic literary life tests and proves genuineness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle suggests that voluntary or involuntary hardship helps purge pride and vanity. Examples: Johnson languishing in garrets, Burns dying as a gauger; poverty may reveal who is genuine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from money/vanity (noncommercial motive)
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer's aim should not be outward profit, pride or vanity; money cannot accomplish the highest work and must be confined to its province.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While financial support may be useful, stipends alone do not make literary quality. A genuine writer must resist vanity and egoism; the work's worth should not be measured solely by money or applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuineness versus spuriousness (avoid being a 'Bungler')
rubrics_metrics.description: A true Literary Man lives wholly in the Divine Idea; partial engagement makes one a 'Bungler', 'Stumper' or 'Nonentity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fichte's disparaging labels are explicit anti-patterns: avoid superficiality, technical competence without inward conviction, or living for social trappings rather than vocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of seriousness and drollery (humour with gravity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good writer can combine true drollery and a 'loving, illuminating laugh' with earnestness; humour need not be mockery or scorn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Knox's vein of drollery — a laugh 'in the eyes' that enlivens rough earnestness. Use humour to humanize and illuminate, not merely to deride.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of medium: mastery of Writing/Printing distinct from Speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing/Printing creates a new kind of hero; writers must master the distinct province of books (the 'true University') even while acknowledging the continuing value of speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the unique reach and permanence of print. The writer should learn to 'read' and to make books that function as repositories and teachers for wide audiences rather than relying only on oral delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public role and institutional responsibility (organization of literary class)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because literature functions as 'our Parliament' and the press supersedes former institutions, writers collectively have a public, political and governing importance; their class should be organized to discharge this role well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle argues for improved social arrangements for Men of Letters (meritocratic support, organizations) and warns that chaotic, chance-driven literary life is the worst regulation. This is a criterion for how society should enable quality literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lasting influence / spiritual endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: The letter of a writer's work dies, but the spirit may live; true literary heroism aims for spiritual endurance and continuing influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Knox's works — 'The letter of his work dies ... but the spirit of it never.' Evaluate works by their power to persist and influence beyond their immediate historical moment.
